Did you take the 3 from the A⁻ ions? A⁻ is the base form, and OH⁻ does not react with it.
That is how many HA molecules reacted. The question asks how many are left.

options.text: 0.20 mol of formic acid with 0.20 mol of KOH
options.message: React them first. With equal moles of formic acid and a strong base, how much formic acid is left afterward?

options.text: 0.20 mol of sodium formate with 0.050 mol of KOH
options.message: Formate ion is the base form, and OH⁻ is a base too. Do they react? Then ask which member of the pair is missing.

options.text: 0.20 mol of formic acid with 0.050 mol of HBr
options.message: Formic acid and HBr are both acids, so nothing here turns formic acid into formate. Which member of the pair is missing?

options.text: 0.20 mol of sodium formate with 0.050 mol of HBr
The OH⁻ reacted with formic acid, and the two amounts are still nearly equal
The OH⁻ reacted with formate ions, which are present in a large amount
options.message: Formate ion is the base form of the pair. A base does not use up another base. Which member has a proton to give to OH⁻?

options.text: The OH⁻ stayed in solution, but a liter of buffer diluted it too far to matter
options.message: If 4 mmol of OH⁻ stayed free in a liter, the pH would be near 11.6. The OH⁻ did not stay as OH⁻. What did it react with?

options.text: The buffer replaced the formic acid that reacted, so neither amount changed
options.message: Nothing replaces what reacts: 4 mmol of one member became 4 mmol of the other. Work out the two new amounts.

options.text: About 4.75, because every concentration has been cut in half
options.message: That is what this dilution does to a strong acid alone. In a buffer, [H₃O⁺] is set by Ka and the two amounts. Which of those did the water change?

options.text: Still about 4.45, because both members were diluted alike
About 5.7, halfway to 7, because half of the liquid is now water
options.message: Water does not pull a buffer toward 7 in proportion to its volume. [H₃O⁺] is set by Ka and the two amounts. Which of those did the water change?

options.text: About 4.15, because the added water brings in more H₃O⁺
options.message: Pure water holds far less H₃O⁺ than this buffer does, so it cannot make it more acidic. Ask what sets [H₃O⁺] in a buffer.

options.text: 90 mmol of Tris and 30 mmol of its conjugate acid, and the pH is a little higher
options.message: H₃O⁺ is an acid, so it reacts with the member that can take a proton. Is that Tris or its conjugate acid? That member goes down.

options.text: 70 mmol of Tris and 40 mmol of its conjugate acid, and the pH is a little lower
options.message: Add up this answer's two amounts. Each H₃O⁺ that reacts turns one particle of one member into one of the other. Can the total of 120 mmol change?

options.text: 80 mmol of Tris and 40 mmol of its conjugate acid, as before, and the pH has not moved
options.message: A buffer does not stop the reaction. Its hold on the pH comes from the reaction: 10 mmol of H₃O⁺ reacted with one member. Which one?

options.text: 70 mmol of Tris and 50 mmol of its conjugate acid, and the pH is a little lower
Between 7.07 and 8.07, below the pKa
Between 8.07 and 9.07, above the pKa
options.message: Decide which member is the acid form before you compare. Tris is the base, so its conjugate acid is the acid form. Which is there more of?

options.text: Exactly 8.07, equal to the pKa
options.message: The pH equals the pKa only when the two amounts are equal. Here they are 0.025 mol and 0.070 mol.

options.text: Between 5.93 and 6.93, near 14.00 − 8.07
options.message: 14.00 − 8.07 is the pKb of Tris. The equation takes the pKa of the acid form as it is, with nothing subtracted from 14.

slips.message: Is the ratio upside down? The base form, formate ion, goes on top, and formic acid goes underneath.
That is the pKa alone. The pH equals the pKa only when the two amounts are equal. Add the logarithm of the ratio.
That is the pH of 0.15 M formic acid with no formate present. The formate ion is there in a large amount, so this is a buffer.
Did you use the natural logarithm? The equation takes the logarithm to base 10, the log key.
That is the logarithm of the ratio alone. Add it to the pKa, 3.75.
Did you round to one decimal place? The pKa has two, so give the pH to two decimal places.

options.text: 5.23 + log(0.080 ÷ 0.24), with the pyridinium ion on top
options.message: Which of the two is the base form? The equation puts the base form over the acid form, whatever charge each one carries.

options.text: 8.77 + log(0.24 ÷ 0.080), with 8.77 from −log Kb
options.message: −log Kb is the pKb of pyridine. The equation is built on the acid form of the pair. Whose pK does it need?

options.text: 5.23 + log(0.24 ÷ 0.080), with pyridine on top
1.7 × 10⁻⁹ + log(0.24 ÷ 0.080), with Kb as the first term
options.message: Kb is a K, not a pK, and the equation is written in logarithms. It needs a pK, and it must be the pK of the pair's acid form.

options.text: Both. Each mixture is made from the same two bottles, so the ratio is 1.5 in each
options.message: The bottles are the same, but the volumes poured are not. Find the millimoles of each form in each mixture, milliliters times molarity, and compare the two ratios.

options.text: Only the first. Equal volumes dilute the two solutions alike
Only the second. In 120.0 mL each solution is diluted less than in 80.0 mL
options.message: Follow each solution into the second mixture: 40.0 mL goes into 120.0 mL, and 80.0 mL goes into 120.0 mL. Are the two diluted alike?

options.text: Neither. Mixing dilutes both solutions, so the bottles' numbers cannot give the ratio
options.message: Mixing does lower both concentrations. The equation takes their ratio. Can two concentrations both fall while their ratio stays where it was?

slips.message: Is the ratio upside down? Glycolate ion, the base form, goes on top.
Did you use 0.200 and 0.500, the concentrations before mixing? Each solution dilutes the other. Find the moles of each member in the mixture.
Did you use the concentrations before mixing, with the acid's on top? Find the moles of each member in the mixture, and put the base form on top.
Did you use the two volumes as the ratio? The ratio is of amounts. Multiply each volume by its molarity to get millimoles.
That is the pKa alone. The two amounts are not equal here, so the logarithm of the ratio is not zero.
Did you round to one decimal place? The pKa has two, so give the pH to two decimal places.
Is the ratio upside down? The wanted pH is below the pKa. Should there be more Tris than conjugate acid, or less?
That is the logarithm of the ratio. Raise 10 to that power to get the ratio itself.
Did you divide the pH by the pKa? Subtract the pKa from the pH first, then raise 10 to that power.
Is that pH − pKa without its sign? The wanted pH is below the pKa, so the logarithm is negative. Then raise 10 to that power.

options.text: P can take more of both, because it holds more moles in all
options.message: A total is not what an addition meets. Added OH⁻ reacts with one member of the pair only, and added H₃O⁺ with the other. Count each member on its own.

options.text: P can take more base, and Q can take more acid
options.message: Added OH⁻ is a base. Which member of a buffer does a base react with, the acid form or the base form? Then compare the moles of that member.

options.text: P can take more acid, and Q can take more base
It cannot be decided without the pKa of formic acid
options.message: A pKa would give each buffer's pH. This question is about amounts: how many moles does each buffer hold of the member that the addition uses up?

options.text: Strong base: it holds more of the member that reacts with OH⁻
Strong acid: Tris is a base, and a base is what reacts with an acid
options.message: Tris does react with acid, but count it: 30 mmol. How much is there of the other member, and what does that one react with?

options.text: The same of either: a buffer holds both members, so it guards both ways alike
options.message: Both ways, yes, but not alike. Each member can use up only as many moles as there are of it. Compare 30 mmol with 90 mmol.

options.text: Strong base: the solution is already basic, so more OH⁻ changes it little
options.message: Capacity is not read from the pH. It is counted in moles: how much of each member is there, and what does each one react with?

slips.message: Did you add the 25 mmol to the acid form? OH⁻ uses up the acid form. Which member grows instead?
That is the Tris after the reaction, which is the base form. The question asks for the acid form.
Did you take the 25 mmol from the Tris? OH⁻ reacts with the acid form, which here is the conjugate acid of Tris.
That is the acid form before the reaction. The OH⁻ reacts with it, mole for mole.
That is in moles. The question asks for millimoles.

options.text: The buffer's ratio of base form to acid form, which the addition has made larger
options.message: A ratio needs both members. Make the table of moles: how much HA is left after the OH⁻ has reacted?

options.text: The 120 mmol of A⁻ alone, a weak base reacting with water
options.message: A⁻ is there, but it is a weak base. Look at the table of moles again for anything stronger that is left.

options.text: The 42 mmol of OH⁻ that was added, all of which is still in the solution
options.message: Not all of it is still there. OH⁻ reacts with HA until one of them runs out. Which runs out, and how much of the other is left?

options.text: The 12 mmol of OH⁻ left over once the HA has run out
Close to 4.87, because a buffer holds its pH
options.message: A buffer needs both members. Make the table of moles: how much propanoic acid is left after 20 mmol of OH⁻ has reacted?

options.text: Between 8 and 9, because a weak base alone is left
Exactly 7, because the acid has been exactly neutralized
options.message: Matched in moles does not mean neutral. Look at what is in the solution after the reaction, and ask whether that ion reacts with water.

options.text: Above 12, because the water beside it goes above 12
options.message: The water goes that high because its OH⁻ has nothing to react with. Here all 20 mmol of OH⁻ reacted. What is left to set the pH?

options.text: H₂PO₄⁻ with HPO₄²⁻, with somewhat more of the acid form
H₂PO₄⁻ with HPO₄²⁻, with somewhat more of the base form
options.message: More base form than acid form puts a buffer's pH above its pKa. Where would this recipe land, and where is 6.90?

options.text: Tris with its conjugate acid, with about fifteen times as much acid form
options.message: This pair could reach pH 6.90, but with so little Tris a small addition of acid would use the base form up. Look for a pKa nearer 6.90.

options.text: Propanoic acid with propanoate ion, with about a hundred times as much base form
options.message: A hundred to one leaves almost no acid form to meet added base. A buffer works best within about one pH unit of its pKa.

options.text: Thallium(I) bromide, TlBr
options.message: Bromide is the conjugate base of HBr, a strong acid. Would Br⁻ take a proton from H₃O⁺?

options.text: Silver iodide, AgI
options.message: Iodide is the conjugate base of HI, a strong acid. Would I⁻ take a proton from H₃O⁺?

options.text: Calcium oxalate, CaC₂O₄
All three, because nitric acid is a strong acid
options.message: The strength of the acid added is not the test. For each solid, ask whether its anion is a base that H₃O⁺ can react with.

options.text: Oxalate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, and acids react with bases
options.message: That statement stops before the solid comes into it. A complete explanation goes on to say what changes in the solution and why more solid dissolves.

options.text: Oxalate is a weak base, so H₃O⁺ turns it into HC₂O₄⁻, Q falls below Ksp and more solid dissolves
The acid raises the Ksp of calcium oxalate, so the water can hold a larger product of ion concentrations than before
options.message: Ksp is a constant at a given temperature, whatever else is in the water. The acid changes a concentration. Which one?

options.text: H₃O⁺ reacts with the calcium ions and removes them, so more solid dissolves
options.message: A calcium ion does not take a proton, so H₃O⁺ leaves it alone. Which ion of the solid is a base?

options.text: [Ni²⁺] is higher, [OH⁻] is lower and Ksp is the same
[Ni²⁺] is higher, [OH⁻] is higher and Ksp is larger
options.message: The acid used up OH⁻, and Ksp is fixed at a given temperature. With those two facts, can both concentrations be higher?

options.text: [Ni²⁺] and [OH⁻] are both back where they started, and Ksp is the same
options.message: If both concentrations were unchanged, no extra solid would have dissolved. What does each formula unit that dissolves put into the solution?

options.text: [Ni²⁺] is higher, [OH⁻] is the same and Ksp is larger
options.message: Look again at Ksp: what would have to change for it to change? Then ask whether [OH⁻] can stay put while acid is using OH⁻ up.

options.text: At pH 10.0, because a hydroxide is most at home in a basic solution
options.message: OH⁻ is one of the ions this solid gives when it dissolves. What does an ion already in the solution do to a salt's solubility (topic 7.12)?

options.text: At pH 8.0, because that buffer holds the least OH⁻
The same in all three, because Ksp is the same in all three
options.message: Ksp is the same in all three, but Ksp is a product of two concentrations. If [OH⁻] differs from buffer to buffer, can [Co²⁺] be the same?

options.text: None dissolves in any of them, because all three buffers are basic
options.message: Basic does not mean saturated. Solid dissolves until the product of the ion concentrations reaches Ksp, and each buffer fixes a different [OH⁻].

options.text: Nickel(II) hydroxide, Ni(OH)₂, is more soluble in dilute nitric acid than in water
options.message: That is true, and it is a hydroxide whose solubility depends on the pH, just as the claim says. Look for a case the claim says cannot happen.

options.text: Cobalt(II) hydroxide, Co(OH)₂, is less soluble in a buffer at pH 10 than in one at pH 8
options.message: True, and it is again a hydroxide answering to the pH, as the claim allows. What kind of solid would the claim be wrong about?

options.text: Silver iodide, AgI, is essentially no more soluble in dilute nitric acid than in water
options.message: True, but a solid that is not a hydroxide and ignores the pH is just what the claim expects. Which of these facts would surprise the classmate?

options.text: Strontium fluoride, SrF₂, is more soluble in dilute nitric acid than in water
[F⁻] is four times what it was, because each PbF₂ that dissolves gives two F⁻
options.message: Each formula unit does give two fluoride ions, but do they all stay as F⁻ in an acidic solution? Then try your answer in the Ksp expression.

options.text: [F⁻] is what it was, because more solid dissolved to replace what the acid took
options.message: If [F⁻] were unchanged while [Pb²⁺] went up four times, the product in the Ksp expression would be four times as large. Can it be, at one temperature?

options.text: [F⁻] is half what it was, because Ksp has not changed
[F⁻] is a quarter of what it was, because [Pb²⁺] times [F⁻] is fixed
options.message: Write the Ksp expression for PbF₂ and look at the power on [F⁻]. Then try your answer in it: does the product come out unchanged?
